lessons.title: After the foothold: the four tactics defenders must see

blocks.md:
A **foothold** is an intruder's first point of control: one account on one machine. In pentest-methodology-recon you saw how authorised testers find that first way in. This course is about everything that happens next, told from the defender's side.

Tiny example: Ana in finance opens a booby-trapped spreadsheet, and malware now runs as Ana on LAPTOP-07. That is all the intruder has. Ana cannot read the payroll database, cannot log in to the domain controller and cannot touch the backups. Real intrusions spend days or weeks turning that one foothold into control of what the intruder came for.

**A real one.** Ireland's Health Service Executive (HSE), the national public health service, commissioned an independent review from PwC (PricewaterhouseCoopers, a professional services and audit firm) after a 2021 ransomware attack. It found that a staff member opened a malicious Excel file from a phishing email on 18 March 2021. The attacker then operated for **eight weeks** before running Conti ransomware (a ransomware-as-a-service operation: its developers let criminal affiliates deploy it) on 14 May 2021.

In between, the incident response firm found the attacker had compromised **180 systems** and many highly privileged accounts across eight organisations and 19 domains (a **domain** is a group of Windows machines managed together, from windows-for-security). More than 2,800 servers and 3,500 workstations showed encryption. Nearly all of the damage came from what happened after the foothold.

To talk about "what happens next" precisely, defenders use **MITRE ATT&CK** (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge), a public knowledge base run by the MITRE Corporation. It sorts attacker behaviour into **tactics** (the goal, the *why*, with IDs starting TA) and **techniques** (the method, the *how*, with IDs starting T). Four tactics cover the post-foothold phase. ATT&CK describes each as a sentence about the adversary:

- **Privilege Escalation** ([TA0004](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0004/)): "trying to gain higher-level permissions", such as root, SYSTEM or local administrator.
- **Credential Access** ([TA0006](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0006/)): "trying to steal account names and passwords".
- **Discovery** ([TA0007](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0007/)): "trying to figure out your environment".
- **Lateral Movement** ([TA0008](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008/)): "trying to move through your environment". *Lateral* means sideways: across to other machines rather than up on the same one.

blocks.title: One foothold becomes a domain compromise

nodes.label:
Helpdesk PC
admin logs in here

scenes.caption: Initial access: malware from an email attachment runs as Ana on LAPTOP-07. Ana is a normal user, so the intruder is too.
Privilege escalation: a misconfiguration or bug on the laptop turns Ana's rights into SYSTEM (TA0004). Only now can the intruder read protected memory.
Credential access and discovery: the intruder takes cached credentials and maps file shares and servers (TA0006, TA0007). Nothing has moved yet.
Lateral movement: a credential stolen on the laptop works on the helpdesk PC, where a domain admin once logged in (TA0008). The loop restarts there.
With a domain admin credential the intruder reaches the domain controller and the backups. Each hop used valid accounts and built-in tools.
Defender view: every hop wrote logon, process and service events. If they reach a central store and someone acts on them, the chain can be cut at any link.

blocks.md:
The steps are a loop, not a line. On each new machine the intruder escalates, collects credentials, looks around and moves again. The US joint advisory on Conti (AA21-265A, by CISA, the FBI, the NSA and, since its March 2022 update, the US Secret Service) describes exactly this: the actors "use tools already available on the victim network" and add tools such as Mimikatz (a public credential-extraction tool) "to obtain users' hashes and clear-text credentials, which enable the actors to escalate privileges within a domain and perform other post-exploitation and lateral movement tasks".

For every technique in this course we ask the same four defender questions:
1. **What does the attacker gain?**
2. **Why does it work?** (which design choice or misconfiguration)
3. **What does it leave behind?** (which log, file or process)
4. **How do we prevent and detect it?**

This course explains mechanisms and audits. It never gives the commands that carry out escalation or movement. Practise only on systems you own or are allowed to test.

blocks.md: The foothold is rarely the disaster. Escalation, credential theft, discovery and lateral movement turn one infected laptop into a domain-wide incident, and each of them leaves evidence on the machines it touches.

blocks.prompt: The HSE's antivirus detected Cobalt Strike and Mimikatz on patient zero on 31 March 2021, six weeks before the ransomware ran. Predict why that detection did not end the intrusion.
blocks.reveal: PwC found the antivirus was set to **monitor mode**, so it recorded the tools but did not block them, and the detection did not start an incident investigation. A detection that nobody acts on is only a log line. Lesson 14 returns to the full HSE timeline and the other warnings that were missed.

blocks.question: An intruder on a workstation runs built-in commands that list domain admins, domain controllers and open file shares. Which ATT&CK tactic is this?
blocks.explain: Listing accounts, servers and shares is Discovery: learning the environment. No privilege changed, no credential was taken and no other machine was entered yet, although the results guide all three.

lessons.title: Linux escalation 1: reading sudo rules like an auditor

blocks.md:
Recall from linux-for-security: a **sudoers** rule says *who* may run *which command* *as whom*. The danger is a rule that grants more than its text suggests.

Tiny example. On web1 the deploy account may run `systemctl restart webapp` as root. That is narrow: one program, fixed arguments. Now add a second rule letting deploy run `less /var/log/webapp/*` as root, to read logs. `less` is a pager, and pagers and editors can start a shell from inside. A shell started by a root `less` is a root shell. The second rule is a full root grant written to look like read access.

**What the attacker gains:** root, from any account (or stolen session) that holds such a rule. ATT&CK files sudo abuse under [T1548.003](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1548/003/).

**Why it works: four ways a rule says more than it means.** All four are documented in the `sudoers(5)` manual.

1. **Programs that run programs.** Editors, pagers, interpreters and many archive tools can start other commands, and those inherit root. The `NOEXEC` tag can stop a dynamically linked program from running further commands, where sudo was built with that support. For editing, `sudoedit` is better: "the editor is run with the permissions of the invoking user".
2. **Wildcards in arguments.** The manual warns they "can match any character, including white space", and in arguments they match `/` too. So `*` can append extra options or `../` paths. Use regular expressions (sudo 1.9.10 and later) or a root-owned wrapper script that takes no arguments.
3. **Commands the user can change.** A rule naming a script that the user can edit hands them root.
4. **The environment.** `env_reset` is on by default. Never add loader variables such as `LD_PRELOAD` (which makes the dynamic linker load a chosen library first, see `ld.so(8)`) to `env_keep`.

blocks.title: Auditing one account's sudo -l output, line by line
blocks.code:
$ sudo -l
Matching Defaults entries for deploy on web1:
    env_reset, mail_badpass, use_pty,
    secure_path=/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin

User deploy may run the following commands on web1:
    (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart webapp
    (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/tar -czf /backup/*.tgz *
    (root) /usr/bin/less /var/log/webapp/*
    (root) NOPASSWD: /opt/webapp/bin/rotate.sh
    (root) sudoedit /etc/webapp/app.conf

scenes.caption: Defaults first: env_reset strips the caller's environment and secure_path fixes PATH, so nothing the caller sets steers what root runs. Good.
One program, fixed arguments. deploy can restart the app and nothing else. This is what a narrow rule looks like.
tar with wildcards: * matches any text, spaces included, so deploy can add any tar options. tar has options that run other programs. Treat as root.
less is a pager that can run shell commands, and the * also matches ../ in the path. Read access via a log group is the right fix.
A script: the rule is only as safe as the file. If deploy can write rotate.sh or its directory, deploy is root. Check owner and mode next (lesson 3).
sudoedit edits a temporary copy with deploy's own permissions, then copies it back. No root editor, no shell escape. This is the safe way to delegate editing.

blocks.md:
How do you know which programs can start other programs? **GTFOBins** is a curated list "of Unix-like executables that can be used to bypass local security restrictions in misconfigured systems", maintained by Emilio Pinna and Andrea Cardaci with other contributors. Attackers use it, so defenders should too: for every program in a sudo rule, look it up. If it is listed as usable under sudo, treat the rule as a root grant and rewrite it.

The manual adds one more trap. Rules like `ALL, !/bin/su` that try to subtract commands from ALL are "advisory at best", because the user can copy the program under another name or escape from an editor.

blocks.code:
# /etc/sudoers.d/deploy   (always edit with: visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/deploy)
Defaults:deploy  env_reset, use_pty, log_output

# restart only, fixed arguments
deploy  web1 = (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart webapp
# backup through a root-owned wrapper; "" means no arguments allowed
deploy  web1 = (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/local/sbin/backup-webapp ""
# config edits run deploy's editor on a copy, not a root editor
deploy  web1 = (root) sudoedit /etc/webapp/app.conf

# Log reading needs no sudo: add deploy to the group that owns
# /var/log/webapp. rotate.sh moved to /usr/local/sbin, owned by root, mode 755.
blocks.caption: The fixed rule set. log_output turns on sudo's I/O logging for this account, so session output is recorded too. An empty-string argument list is documented in sudoers(5) as 'no arguments'.

blocks.md:
**What it leaves behind.** sudo logs every command it runs, with the user, working directory and full command line (you saw the line format in linux-for-security). A sudo log line for `less` or `tar` is normal; a **root shell whose parent process is less, vim or tar** is not. Process-tree rules that alert on shells spawned by pagers, editors or archivers under sudo catch this class. With `log_output`, sudo also records what appeared on screen.

**Prevent:** grant commands, not programs; no wildcards in arguments; `sudoedit` for files; wrappers owned by root; review every rule against GTFOBins. **Detect:** forward sudo logs off the host, alert on unexpected children of sudo-run programs, and diff sudoers files against a reviewed baseline.

Misconception: "NOPASSWD is the dangerous part." It does remove a hurdle for an intruder who has a shell but not the password (a web shell, a stolen SSH key). But a rule that leads to a shell is a root grant with or without a password prompt. Fix what the command can do first, then decide on the password.

**Even perfect rules sit on top of the sudo program itself.** Baron Samedit (CVE-2021-3156), which you met in os-security-isolation, was a heap overflow in sudo disclosed by Qualys on 26 January 2021. Qualys reported it was "exploitable by any local user", including users not listed in sudoers at all, in sudo 1.8.2 to 1.8.31p2 and 1.9.0 to 1.9.5p1 in their default configuration. The bug had been present since July 2011. The audit of a host therefore always includes the sudo version, not just its rules.

blocks.question: Which sudoers line gives the least room for escalation?
blocks.explain: sudoedit runs alice's editor with alice's own permissions on a copy. vim as root can start a shell; find with a wildcard can take extra arguments, and find can run commands; subtracting programs from ALL is advisory at best, as the manual says.

blocks.question: A sudo rule allows `/opt/app/bin/rotate.sh` as root. The file is owned by root with mode 755, but `/opt/app/bin` is owned by the app user, who holds the rule. Is the rule safe?
options: Yes, the file is owned by root and not writable by others
No: whoever can write the directory can rename the file and put their own rotate.sh in its place
Yes, because sudo checks the file's owner before running it
blocks.explain: Write permission on a directory lets you create, delete and rename entries in it (linux-for-security). The app user can replace rotate.sh with a new file. sudo does not check ownership of the target by default, so the directory must be root-owned too.

lessons.title: Linux escalation 2: jobs, scripts and paths that root trusts

blocks.md:
One rule covers a whole family of Linux escalations: **if root runs it and you can change it, you are root.**

Tiny example. `/etc/cron.d/report` says `*/5 * * * * root /opt/report/build.sh`: every five minutes cron runs build.sh as root. The file belongs to the report user with mode 775. Anyone who can write it (the report user, or anyone in its group) decides what root does within five minutes. Cron runs a job with the privileges named in the job, not those of the file's owner, so the file's weak permissions become root's problem.

**What the attacker gains:** root code execution on a schedule, which doubles as persistence. ATT&CK lists cron abuse as [T1053.003](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1053/003/).

**Where root's trust hides.** Each of these is a place where root runs something that someone else might control:

- **System crontabs**: `/etc/crontab` and files in `/etc/cron.d/`. These are system jobs, and unlike user tables they carry a user field (`crontab(5)`). Also the directories run by `run-parts`, such as `/etc/cron.daily`.
- **Root's own crontab**, stored under `/var/spool/cron/` (Debian and Ubuntu use a `crontabs` subdirectory).
- **systemd units and timers** whose `ExecStart=` runs as root because no `User=` is set (linux-for-security showed unit files).
- **What those scripts touch**: files they `source`, programs they call by a bare name and directories in their `PATH`. A writable directory early in PATH lets someone plant a program with the same name.
- **Missing targets**: a job pointing at a file that no longer exists. Whoever can create it controls root.
- **The directory, not just the file**: write permission on a directory lets you replace any file inside it.

blocks.title: An audit script finds root's cron targets that others can change
blocks.code:
#!/bin/bash
# root-cron-targets.sh: programs root's cron runs, and who else can change them
# Linux only, read-only. Run as root so every crontab is readable.
targets() {
  for f in /etc/crontab /etc/cron.d/*; do      # system tables: 5 times, USER, command
    [ -f "$f" ] && awk '!/^[[:space:]]*#/ && NF >= 7 && $6 == "root" && substr($7, 1, 1) == "/" { print $7 }' "$f"
  done
  for f in /var/spool/cron/root /var/spool/cron/crontabs/root; do   # root's own table: no user field
    [ -f "$f" ] && awk '!/^[[:space:]]*#/ && NF >= 6 && substr($6, 1, 1) == "/" { print $6 }' "$f"
  done
}
targets | sort -u | while read -r t; do
  if [ ! -e "$t" ]; then echo "MISSING $t  (whoever can create it controls root)"; continue; fi
  for p in "$t" "$(dirname "$t")"; do
    owner=$(stat -c %U "$p"); mode=$(stat -c %a "$p")
    if [ "$owner" != root ] || (( 8#$mode & 8#022 )); then
      echo "RISK    $p  owner=$owner mode=$mode"
    fi
  done
done

scenes.caption: System tables have a user field in column 6. awk keeps lines where that field is root and the command (column 7) is an absolute path.
Root's personal crontab has no user field, so the command is column 6. Each file is checked for existence first, because some awk versions stop at a missing file.
build.sh exists. The script checks the file and then its directory: owner must be root and the group and other write bits (octal 022) must be clear.
Owner is report and the group write bit is set, so it is reported. The directory /opt/report is root 755 and passes.
backup.sh and its directory are root-owned with mode 755: nothing printed. cleanup.sh does not exist at all, which is its own finding.
scenes.output:
RISK    /opt/report/build.sh  owner=report mode=775
MISSING /usr/local/bin/cleanup.sh  (whoever can create it controls root)

blocks.code:
# /etc/crontab (excerpt)
30 2  * * *  root  /usr/local/bin/backup.sh
# /etc/cron.d/report
*/5 *  * * *  root  /opt/report/build.sh --quiet
# root's crontab
0 3  * * *  /usr/local/bin/cleanup.sh

$ sudo ./root-cron-targets.sh
RISK    /opt/report/build.sh  owner=report mode=775
MISSING /usr/local/bin/cleanup.sh  (whoever can create it controls root)
blocks.caption: The input the trace used and the script's real output (tested on a mock tree). Simplified: it skips @reboot lines and commands run through cd or a shell wrapper, so read those by hand.

blocks.prompt: A root cron job runs `/srv/tools/sync.sh`. The file is owned by root with mode 755, but `/srv/tools` is mode 777. Is this safe, and does the script above report it?
blocks.reveal: **Not safe.** With write permission on `/srv/tools`, any user can delete or rename `sync.sh` and create a new one with the same name, which root then runs. That is why the script checks `dirname` as well as the file: it prints `RISK /srv/tools owner=root mode=777`, because the other-write bit (part of 022) is set even though the owner is root.

blocks.md:
**What it leaves behind.** A change to a root-run file is a file-modification event: watches in auditd (the Linux audit daemon, which records kernel audit events; `auditctl -w <file> -p wa` watches a file for writes and attribute changes) or a file-integrity monitor record the write and the process that made it. Cron logs each job it starts to syslog or the journal. After the change, root's job behaves differently: new child processes under cron, outbound connections from a script that never made any.

**Prevent:** everything root runs, and every directory above it, is owned by root and not group or world writable; jobs that do not need root run under their own user (cron's user field, systemd `User=`); scripts use absolute paths and set their own `PATH`. **Detect:** run the audit on a schedule, keep hashes of root-run scripts as a baseline (linux-for-security), and alert on writes to them.

The same rule covers the files that define privilege themselves. A writable `/etc/passwd`, `/etc/shadow`, `/etc/sudoers.d/` entry or systemd unit directory is instant root. Treat any group or world write bit under `/etc` or `/usr` as a finding.

blocks.question: A systemd service runs `ExecStart=/home/dev/tools/agent` and its unit has no `User=` line. Developers can edit files in their home directories. What is the best fix?
options: Move the binary to a root-owned directory and run the service as a dedicated unprivileged user
blocks.explain: Without User=, the service runs as root, so whoever controls the file controls root. Moving it to a root-owned path removes the write path, and running as its own user limits the damage even if something else goes wrong. NoNewPrivileges does not help when the process already is root.

blocks.question: Why does the audit script also print targets that do not exist?
options: A missing file makes cron crash
Whoever can create a file at that path decides what root runs
Missing files are a sign the system was already compromised
blocks.explain: cron will run whatever appears at that path, as root. If any non-root user can create the file (check the directory), the job is an escalation waiting to happen. It is usually an old job someone forgot to remove.

lessons.title: Linux escalation 3: setuid, capabilities, kernel bugs, docker group

blocks.md:
Some privilege is attached to files and groups rather than written in a rule. Four classes remain on Linux, each paired with the check that finds it.

Tiny example. Years ago someone fixed a permission problem by copying an interpreter to `/usr/local/bin/py-admin` and setting the setuid bit on it. Every user on the machine can now run Python as root. No sudo rule, no cron job: a single mode bit.

**1. Setuid binaries that should not be setuid.** You know the mechanism from linux-for-security: a setuid-root program runs as root whoever starts it. Two risks follow. A **non-vendor setuid file** (a copied shell or interpreter, a vendor tool installed by hand) can grant root by design. A **vendor setuid program with a bug** grants root by accident: PwnKit (CVE-2021-4034, pkexec, disclosed 25 January 2022) and Baron Samedit (sudo) were both setuid-root programs that any local user could exploit.

**Check:** list every setuid and setgid file and compare it with the package database; anything no package installed needs a reason. Mount user-writable filesystems with **nosuid**, which the `mount(8)` manual says makes the kernel "not honor set-user-ID and set-group-ID bits or file capabilities" for programs there.

**2. File capabilities.** Capabilities (os-security-isolation) split root into pieces. Some pieces are root in disguise: `CAP_SETUID` lets a process "make arbitrary manipulations of process UIDs", and `CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE` bypasses file permission checks. Either one on an interpreter or shell is a root grant.

blocks.code:
#!/bin/bash
# privesc-inventory.sh: read-only checks for classes 1 to 4 (Debian/Ubuntu; run as root)

# 1. setuid/setgid files that no package installed
find / -xdev -type f \( -perm -4000 -o -perm -2000 \) 2>/dev/null |
while read -r f; do
  dpkg -S "$f" >/dev/null 2>&1 || echo "NOT FROM A PACKAGE: $f"
done

# 2. files carrying capabilities (expect a short list such as ping)
getcap -r / 2>/dev/null

# 3. running kernel versus the newest one installed
echo "running: $(uname -r)"; ls /boot/vmlinuz-* 2>/dev/null

# 4. who can drive the Docker daemon (root-equivalent)
getent group docker
ls -l /var/run/docker.sock 2>/dev/null
blocks.caption: On RPM systems use `rpm -qf` instead of `dpkg -S`. On merged-/usr systems dpkg may know a file only by its /bin path, so check each hit by hand before acting.

blocks.md:
**3. Kernel bugs.** The kernel enforces every check, so one kernel bug can bypass all of them, for every process and every container on the host. Dirty COW (2016) and Dirty Pipe (2022), from earlier courses, both let an unprivileged user write to files they could only read.

**Check:** compare the *running* kernel with your vendor's fixed version. A common trap is a patched kernel package that was installed but never booted: `uname -r` still shows the old one. Reboot after kernel updates, or use your distribution's live-patching service.

**4. Group memberships that equal root.** Docker's documentation is blunt: the daemon "always runs as the root user", it creates a Unix socket "accessible by members of the docker group", and "the docker group grants root-level privileges to the user". The reason, also from Docker's docs: you can start a container whose `/host` directory is the host's `/`, and "the container can alter your host filesystem without any restriction". ATT&CK lists this kind of escape as [T1611](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1611/).

blocks.title: Why the docker group is root-equivalent

nodes.label:
rootless mode or
no group membership

scenes.caption: A developer is added to the docker group so they can skip sudo. Group membership gives their processes access to the daemon's socket.
The daemon runs as root and does what the API asks, including starting a container with the host's root directory mounted inside it.
Inside that container, writes to the mounted directory land on the host as root. No bug was needed: the feature works as documented.
Defences: treat docker group membership as root in access reviews, prefer rootless mode, and log container creation with host mounts.

blocks.md:
**What these classes leave behind.** A new setuid file is a change you can catch by diffing the inventory against yesterday's. Capability changes show up in the same diff. Kernel exploits often crash or leave kernel messages, but not reliably. Container abuse appears as container creation with host paths mounted, in the daemon's events and your audit logs.

PwnKit shows the limit of logs. Qualys noted that the public exploitation technique leaves traces in syslog (messages that the SHELL value was not found in `/etc/shells`, or that an environment variable contains suspicious content), and then warned that the bug "is also exploitable without leaving any traces in the logs". Inventory, patch level and removing needless setuid bits are the controls; logs are a bonus.

blocks.question: A contractor's account is in the docker group but has no sudo rights. How should an access review classify it?
options: Unprivileged: no sudo means no root
Root-equivalent: the docker group can start containers that write the host filesystem as root
Low risk unless the account also has a password
blocks.explain: Docker's own documentation says the docker group grants root-level privileges, because the root daemon will mount the host filesystem into a container on request. Review it exactly like a sudo ALL rule.

blocks.question: Your patch tool reports that the fixed kernel for Dirty Pipe was installed yesterday. `uname -r` shows the old version. What is the state of the host?
options: Still vulnerable: the old kernel is the one running until a reboot or live patch
Partly protected: half the kernel is updated
blocks.explain: The kernel in memory is the one that booted. Installing a new kernel package changes files in /boot, not the running code. Until the host reboots into it, or a live patch is applied, the bug is still there.

lessons.title: Windows escalation 1: unquoted paths and weak service permissions

blocks.md:
**Why unquoted paths are ambiguous.** Services are started through `CreateProcess`, and Microsoft's documentation for it explains the problem. When the program name is not given separately, the first white-space-delimited token of the command line is taken as the program. With a long file name that contains a space and no quotes, "the file name is ambiguous". For the string `c:\program files\sub dir\program name`, the documentation lists the order the system tries:

1. `c:\program.exe`
2. `c:\program files\sub.exe`
3. `c:\program files\sub dir\program.exe`
4. `c:\program files\sub dir\program name.exe`

The first file that exists wins. **What the attacker gains:** if they can create a file at an earlier position, their program runs instead, as the service's account.

blocks.title: How Windows resolves one unquoted service path
blocks.code:
ImagePath (no quotes), service runs as LocalSystem:
C:\Program Files\Acme Corp\Agent Service\agent.exe -service

Candidates, tried in order until one exists:
1  C:\Program.exe
2  C:\Program Files\Acme.exe
3  C:\Program Files\Acme Corp\Agent.exe
4  C:\Program Files\Acme Corp\Agent Service\agent.exe

Folder ACL (icacls):
C:\Program Files\Acme Corp  BUILTIN\Users:(OI)(CI)(M)

scenes.caption: The path has three spaces before .exe and no quotes, so Windows cannot tell where the file name ends. Each space is a possible end.
Candidates 1 and 2 sit in folders whose ACLs normally keep users out. They do not exist, so Windows moves on.
Candidate 3 lives in Acme Corp. An installer gave Users Modify (M) on that folder, so any user can create Agent.exe there.
If Agent.exe appears, it runs as SYSTEM at the next service start, before the real agent.exe is ever tried. Quoting the path and fixing the ACL each close this.

blocks.code:
# Read-only: services whose path is unquoted and has white space before the first .exe
Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_Service |
  Where-Object PathName -NotMatch '^\s*"' |
  Where-Object PathName -Match '^(?:(?!\.exe)\S)*\s.*\.exe' |
  Select-Object Name, StartName, StartMode, PathName

# Fix (as an administrator): store the path with quotes around the executable
Set-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\AcmeAgent' -Name ImagePath `
  -Value '"C:\Program Files\Acme Corp\Agent Service\agent.exe" -service'
blocks.caption: The regular expression walks non-space characters up to the first .exe and reports the path if white space comes first. Service settings live under the Services registry key (ATT&CK T1574.011). A finding is only exploitable if a user can write an earlier folder, so pair it with the ACL check below.

blocks.md:
**Weak service permissions.** A service is itself a securable object with a DACL (windows-for-security). Microsoft's page on service access rights singles out **SERVICE_CHANGE_CONFIG**: "Because this grants the caller the right to change the executable file that the system runs, it should be granted only to administrators." **WRITE_DAC** and **WRITE_OWNER** are just as bad, because they let the holder grant themselves that right. The same applies to the service's registry key: ATT&CK notes that weak permissions there let someone point `ImagePath` at a program they control.

**Weak file permissions** are the third route: if the executable or its folder is writable, replace the file. The checks below cover all three routes.

blocks.code:
# Read-only: which SYSTEM services run which files?
Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_Service -Filter "StartName='LocalSystem'" |
  Select-Object Name, PathName

# Then, for each executable and the folder that holds it:
icacls "C:\Program Files\Acme Corp\Agent Service\agent.exe"
icacls "C:\Program Files\Acme Corp"
# A finding is any entry for Everyone, BUILTIN\Users, NT AUTHORITY\Authenticated Users
# or NT AUTHORITY\INTERACTIVE that includes (F) full, (M) modify, (W) write,
# or the specific rights (WD) create files or (AD) create folders.

# The service object's own security descriptor, in SDDL form
sc.exe sdshow AcmeAgent
blocks.caption: sdshow prints SDDL (Security Descriptor Definition Language, a text form of the DACL), one ACE per bracket such as (A;;CCLCRP;;;AU). A finding: a non-admin trustee (AU, BU, IU, or WD for Everyone) holding DC (change config), WD (write DAC), WO (write owner), GA or GW.

blocks.md: Run the path audit and the ACL audit together. An unquoted path with no writable folder before it is a hygiene fix; with one, it is a working escalation to SYSTEM.

blocks.question: A service's ImagePath is `C:\Tools\Log Shipper\ship.exe`, unquoted, and users can create files in `C:\Tools`. Which file would run as the service's account if a user created it?
blocks.explain: The first space falls after Log, so Windows first tries `C:\Tools\Log.exe`, and that folder is writable. `C:\Log.exe` is never a candidate because the path does not break at the root, and Shipper.exe is not a prefix of the path.

blocks.question: Which right on a service object, granted to ordinary users, amounts to giving them SYSTEM?
blocks.explain: SERVICE_CHANGE_CONFIG lets the holder change the executable the service runs; Microsoft says it should be granted only to administrators. The other three only read status or dependency information.

lessons.title: Windows escalation 2: AlwaysInstallElevated and token privileges

blocks.md:
Two more Windows classes have nothing to do with files: a **policy** that elevates every install, and **privileges** in a token that are one step from SYSTEM.

Tiny example. A school's IT team wanted pupils to install approved software without calling the helpdesk, so they switched on a Group Policy that makes Windows Installer always install with elevated privileges. It worked. It also meant any pupil could install *any* package, with SYSTEM rights.

**AlwaysInstallElevated.** Windows Installer is the Windows component that installs `.msi` packages. Microsoft's documentation for the AlwaysInstallElevated policy says it installs a package "with elevated (system) privileges" when the value is 1 under **both** `HKEY_CURRENT_USER` and `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE` (`Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer`), and warns: "This option is equivalent to granting full administrative rights, which can pose a massive security risk. Microsoft strongly discourages the use of this setting."

**Why it works:** an installer package can run programs while it installs. ATT&CK's entry for `msiexec.exe` ([T1218.007](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218/007/)) notes that its execution "may also be elevated to SYSTEM privileges if the AlwaysInstallElevated policy is enabled". **What it leaves behind:** Windows Installer activity in the Application log, and a process tree in which `msiexec.exe` running as SYSTEM starts children that no approved package would.

blocks.code:
# Read-only: AlwaysInstallElevated is active only when BOTH values are 1.
# Each command prints the value if it is set and nothing if it is not.
Get-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer' `
  -Name AlwaysInstallElevated -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Get-ItemProperty -Path 'HKCU:\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer' `
  -Name AlwaysInstallElevated -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

# Which privileges does this process's token hold, and are they enabled?
whoami /priv
blocks.caption: Fix: remove the policy (or set it to 0) through the same Group Policy that set it, and deliver software with a deployment tool instead. A privilege listed as Disabled in whoami /priv can still be enabled by the process that holds it.

blocks.md:
**Token privileges.** Recall from windows-for-security: privileges live in the access token and apply system-wide. A handful are effectively SYSTEM:
- **SeDebugPrivilege** ("Debug programs"): attach to and read any process, including LSASS. By default only Administrators hold it, and Microsoft advises assigning it "only to trusted users".
- **SeBackupPrivilege** and **SeRestorePrivilege**: read or write any file regardless of its DACL.
- **SeLoadDriverPrivilege**: load kernel drivers (lesson 7 shows why that matters).
- **SeImpersonatePrivilege** ("Impersonate a client after authentication"): the subtle one.

**Impersonation**, in Microsoft's words, is "the ability of a thread to run in a security context that is different from the context of the process that owns the thread". It exists so a server can do work *as its client*: when a file server thread impersonates Ana, access checks use Ana's token.

blocks.title: SeImpersonatePrivilege: the server becomes whoever connects

scenes.caption: A service account (say a web app pool) holds SeImpersonatePrivilege, as all services started by the service control manager do by default.
A client connects to the service, for example over a named pipe or RPC, and authenticates. The service now holds a token for that client.
Normal use: the thread impersonates the client so that access checks run as the client. For an ordinary client that restricts what the server can do.
Abuse: if the attacker controls the service and can get a SYSTEM process to connect, impersonation hands them a SYSTEM context. Microsoft's policy page describes exactly this risk.

blocks.md:
Microsoft's page for this user right explains why it is restricted: without the requirement, "an unauthorized user" could "cause a client to connect" to a service they created and impersonate that client, which "could elevate the unauthorized user's permissions to administrative or system levels". By default the right belongs to Administrators, Local Service, Network Service and Service, and services started by the service control manager get the Service group added to their tokens.

The defender's consequence: **a compromised service account is often one step from SYSTEM.** A web shell running as an IIS (Internet Information Services) app pool identity already holds the privilege.

**What it leaves behind:** Security event **4672** ("Special privileges assigned to new logon") lists sensitive privileges, including SeImpersonatePrivilege, granted at logon. Process trees show the payoff: a shell or new SYSTEM process descended from a web worker or database process.

Prevent: keep this user right at its defaults (Microsoft's countermeasure for member servers is to grant it only to Administrators and the service groups); never grant SeDebug, SeBackup or SeLoadDriver to ordinary accounts; patch and harden internet-facing services, because their accounts already hold SeImpersonate. Detect: alert on shells and LOLBins (built-in Windows programs that can be misused, explained next) whose parent is a web or database worker process.

**LOLBins** in that callout are "living off the land" binaries: programs that ship with Windows and can be misused, catalogued by the LOLBAS project (Living Off The Land Binaries, Scripts and Libraries). Like GTFOBins on Linux, the list is useful to defenders because it names the built-in programs that deserve alerts when an unusual parent starts them.

blocks.question: On a workstation, AlwaysInstallElevated is 1 under HKLM but not set under HKCU. What does Windows Installer do for a package a user brings in?
options: Installs it with the user's own privileges, because elevation requires both values
Asks for UAC consent and then installs as SYSTEM
blocks.explain: Microsoft's documentation requires the value 1 under both keys. Otherwise managed applications get elevation and unmanaged ones install with the user's privileges. Audit both keys, and remove the policy rather than relying on one half being unset.

blocks.question: An attacker uploads a web shell to an IIS server; it runs as the app pool identity. Why do defenders treat this as close to SYSTEM compromise?
options: App pool identities are members of Administrators
IIS runs every request as SYSTEM
Service identities hold SeImpersonatePrivilege by default, which turns a connecting SYSTEM client into SYSTEM code
blocks.explain: Processes started as services get the Service group and with it SeImpersonatePrivilege. If the attacker can make a privileged client connect to something they control, impersonation gives them that client's rights. That is why web servers need patching, least-privilege identities and process-tree alerting.

lessons.title: Windows escalation 3: UAC bypass, vulnerable drivers, PrintNightmare

blocks.md:
Some lines on Windows look like security boundaries but are not treated as boundaries by Microsoft. Knowing which is which tells a defender where an attacker's next step is cheap.

Microsoft's published **Windows security servicing criteria** list what it promises to fix. **User Account Control** appears in the table of defence-in-depth features, with no promise to service bypasses. And for the NT kernel the criteria state: "Administrator-to-kernel is not a security boundary." Administrators are part of the trusted computing base (TCB: the parts of the system that must be trusted for its security to hold) and "can disable security features". So two steps are cheap once an attacker is an administrator: getting a high-integrity token without a prompt, and getting code into the kernel.

**UAC bypass as a class.** Recall the split token from windows-for-security: an administrator's programs run with a filtered, medium-integrity token until a consent prompt elevates them. A **UAC bypass** gets the full token *without* that prompt. ATT&CK ([T1548.002](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1548/002/)) explains the usual route: unless UAC is set to its highest level, "certain Windows programs can elevate privileges or execute some elevated Component Object Model objects without prompting". If such an auto-elevating program reads something the user controls (a registry key under HKCU, a file path), the user steers what runs at high integrity. ATT&CK names `eventvwr.exe` as one documented example of an auto-elevating program that has been misused, which is why defenders watch what such programs start.

**What the attacker gains:** high integrity, from an account that is already an administrator. A standard user has no administrator token to unlock, so there is nothing to bypass.

**Prevent:** give people standard accounts for daily work and separate admin accounts (lesson 10), and set UAC to *Always notify* where admins must work locally. **Detect:** in 4688, the Token Elevation Type field (windows-for-security) shows a full token; combine it with the parent process. An auto-elevating Microsoft program that starts an unexpected child, especially right after a Sysmon **event 13** registry write under the user's HKCU classes, is the classic pattern.

**Bring your own vulnerable driver (BYOVD).** Microsoft has "strict requirements for code running in kernel", including driver signing. ATT&CK ([T1068](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1068/)) records the workaround: attackers bring a driver that is **legitimately signed but has a bug**, load it with admin rights, then use the bug to run their code in the kernel. Its examples include BlackByte 2.0 ransomware using a flaw in the RTCore64.sys driver (CVE-2019-16098) for "privilege escalation and defense evasion" (avoiding or disabling security tools; ATT&CK now files this under its Stealth and Defense Impairment tactics). Microsoft's own page states the trend: "malicious actors are turning to exploit vulnerabilities in legitimate and signed kernel drivers".

blocks.title: BYOVD: from administrator to kernel, and the blocklist

nodes.label:
Signed driver
with a known bug

scenes.caption: The attacker already has administrator rights (and with them SeLoadDriverPrivilege). Administrator-to-kernel is not a boundary Microsoft services.
The driver is genuinely signed, so Windows loads it. Its bug lets the attacker run code or write memory in the kernel.
From the kernel the attacker can remove the hooks that EDR (endpoint detection and response: per-host security software, lesson 14) and antivirus rely on.

Defence: the vulnerable driver blocklist (on by default since the Windows 11 2022 update, also enforced when HVCI, memory integrity, is on) refuses known-bad drivers, and Sysmon event 6 logs every driver load with hash and signature.

blocks.md:
**BYOVD defences** from Microsoft's recommended driver block rules page: the vulnerable driver blocklist "is enabled by default for all devices" since the Windows 11 2022 update, and is also enforced when **memory integrity**, also called **HVCI** (hypervisor-protected code integrity: the hypervisor checks code before the kernel may run it), Smart App Control or S mode is on. HVCI "is on by-default for most new Windows 11 devices". Microsoft also recommends the attack surface reduction rule *Block abuse of exploited vulnerable signed drivers*, which stops the driver being written to disk, and warns the blocklist "isn't guaranteed to block every driver found to have vulnerabilities".

**What it leaves behind:** Sysmon **event 6** (driver loaded, with hashes and signature), and a new kernel-driver service: Security event **4697** records service type `0x1` (kernel driver) and, as its documentation notes, kernel drivers have no service account logged. Compare loaded driver hashes against Microsoft's blocklist.

blocks.code:
# Read-only: the last 20 driver loads Sysmon saw (event 6), with signer and hashes
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{ LogName = 'Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational'; Id = 6 } -MaxEvents 20 |
  Select-Object TimeCreated, Message

# Read-only: PrintNightmare-era Point and Print hardening (1 or absent = admins only)
Get-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Printers\PointAndPrint' `
  -Name RestrictDriverInstallationToAdministrators -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
blocks.caption: Both queries change nothing. Sysmon must be installed for the first one; the second reads the registry value described in Microsoft's KB5005652.

blocks.md:
**Case: PrintNightmare (CVE-2021-34527).** You saw the basics in windows-for-security. Read it now as a *class*: a service running as SYSTEM exposes a privileged operation to ordinary users. CISA's Emergency Directive 21-04 (13 July 2021) says the Print Spooler "improperly performs privileged file operations and fails to restrict access to functionality that allows users to add printers and related drivers", letting "a remote authenticated attacker" run code with SYSTEM privileges. Agencies had to stop the spooler on all domain controllers by 14 July and install the July updates by 20 July 2021.

Microsoft then changed a default: since the updates of 10 August 2021, installing printer drivers through Point and Print requires administrator rights (KB5005652). It warns that setting `RestrictDriverInstallationToAdministrators` to 0 "makes devices vulnerable". The Conti advisory reports that a leaked Conti playbook told affiliates to use PrintNightmare to escalate and move laterally.

blocks.question: A user with a standard (non-admin) account runs a published UAC bypass. What happens?
options: They get a high-integrity administrator token
Nothing useful: a standard user has no administrator token for the bypass to unlock
UAC is disabled for all users on the machine
blocks.explain: UAC bypasses skip the consent prompt between an administrator's filtered token and full token. A standard user has only one, unprivileged token. That is why standard accounts for daily work blunt this whole class.

blocks.question: Why does a vulnerable but signed driver get past Windows' requirement that kernel drivers be signed?
options: Because signing only proves who published the driver, not that the driver is free of bugs
Because administrators can turn off signature checks with no reboot
Because the blocklist only covers unsigned drivers
blocks.explain: A signature binds code to a publisher. A legitimately signed driver with a flaw still loads, and its flaw does the attacker's work. Blocking by hash or version, as the vulnerable driver blocklist does, is the fix.

lessons.title: Credentials are the real currency: where they live on a host

blocks.md:
Escalation gets an intruder one machine. **Credentials** (anything that proves an identity: passwords, password hashes, Kerberos tickets, private keys, cloud tokens) get them every machine that accepts those credentials.

Tiny example. A helpdesk administrator signs in to Ana's laptop to fix a printer and leaves. For single sign-on, Windows keeps credential material for that session in LSASS memory (windows-for-security). An intruder who later becomes SYSTEM on the laptop can take it and sign in as the helpdesk admin to hundreds of other machines. Microsoft's guidance on secure workstations puts it plainly: "An attacker who compromises a PC or device can impersonate or steal credentials/tokens for all accounts that use it."

**Why credential theft beats exploits**, from the attacker's side:
- **It looks like work.** A valid account using normal admin tools blends in. ATT&CK says lateral movement with "legitimate credentials with native network and operating system tools" may be stealthier.
- **Patching does not stop it.** CISA's analysis of NotPetya (2017) found the first and "in most cases" most effective way it spread was a modified Mimikatz stealing Windows credentials, then using WMIC or PsExec to reach other systems. The EternalBlue exploit was a second method, for *unpatched* machines only. Credentials reached the patched ones too.
- **Nothing crashes.** Exploits can fail and leave crash dumps; a correct password just works.

The Conti advisory makes the same point from 2021: hashes and clear-text credentials "enable the actors to escalate privileges within a domain".

blocks.title: Where credentials live on one Windows laptop, and who can read them

nodes.label:
Scripts, config files,
GPP files in SYSVOL

SSH private keys,
cloud CLI tokens

scenes.caption: Seven places credential material commonly sits. The question for each is: what level of access does an intruder need to read it?
LSASS memory and the SAM hive need administrator or SYSTEM rights (ATT&CK T1003.001, T1003.002). This is why escalation usually comes first.
The browser store is decrypted with the user's own logon credentials (T1555.003), so any code running as the user can read it. No escalation needed.
Files, keys and tokens need only read access to wherever they were left (T1552.001, T1552.004). Group Policy Preferences files in SYSVOL are readable by every domain user.
On a cloud VM, any process that can reach the metadata service can ask it for the instance role's temporary credentials (T1552.005).

blocks.md:
Details a defender needs for each store:

- **LSASS** ([T1003.001](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/)): after logon, the system "generates and stores a variety of credential materials in LSASS process memory". Protections: LSA protection and Credential Guard (windows-for-security, and lesson 10). Signal: Sysmon **event 10**, a process opening LSASS.
- **SAM** ([T1003.002](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/002/)): local account hashes; reading it "requires SYSTEM level access". A stolen local hash matters only where the same password is reused, which lesson 10 removes.
- **Browser stores** ([T1555.003](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/)): Windows' `CryptUnprotectData` decrypts them using "the victim's cached logon credentials as the decryption key".

- **Files** ([T1552.001](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/001/)): passwords in scripts, configuration and backups. **Group Policy Preferences** ([T1552.006](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/006/)) once let admins push passwords to machines; they sit in SYSVOL (a folder on every domain controller, shared with the whole domain, that holds Group Policy files), which "any domain user can view", encrypted with a key that "has been made public". Microsoft's MS14-025 update (2014) stopped new ones being saved and recommends removing any that still exist.

- **Cloud metadata** ([T1552.005](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/005/)): a cloud VM can ask a local web service about itself (on AWS, the **Instance Metadata Service**, IMDS, at 169.254.169.254), including temporary credentials for the role attached to the instance. ATT&CK notes it is "accessible by anyone who can access the instance", which includes a web application tricked into making requests for an attacker (server-side request forgery, SSRF).

AWS's defence is **IMDSv2**, a "session-oriented" version: a client must first get a session token with a PUT request, PUT requests carrying an `X-Forwarded-For` header (a header proxies add) are rejected, and by default the token response has an IP hop limit of 1, so it cannot travel past the instance. AWS describes it as defence in depth "against open firewalls, reverse proxies, and SSRF vulnerabilities". You can make an instance accept only IMDSv2.

blocks.code:
# Defender checks (run by admins). Nothing here reads anyone's secrets.

# 1. Require IMDSv2 session tokens on an EC2 instance (AWS CLI)
aws ec2 modify-instance-metadata-options \
    --instance-id i-1234567890abcdef0 \
    --http-tokens required \
    --http-endpoint enabled

# 2. Find old Group Policy Preferences files that still carry a password field
#    (PowerShell, any domain-joined machine; MS14-025 calls it the CPassword attribute)
Get-ChildItem -Path "\\$env:USERDNSDOMAIN\SYSVOL" -Recurse -Filter *.xml -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
  Select-String -Pattern 'cpassword' -List | Select-Object Path
blocks.caption: The first command is AWS's documented way to require IMDSv2 on an existing instance. For the second, Microsoft's KB2962486 (MS14-025) provides a script that finds such preferences; delete them and change any password they held.

blocks.md: Misconception: "we have MFA, so stolen hashes and tickets don't matter." Multi-factor authentication protects the sign-in that asks for it, usually remote access and cloud portals. Inside a Windows network, NTLM and Kerberos authentication to a file server or another workstation uses the hash or ticket directly and does not prompt for a second factor.

blocks.question: An intruder has code running as an ordinary user on a laptop, with no admin rights yet. Which store can they most likely read immediately?
blocks.explain: Browser stores have traditionally been decrypted with the user's own logon credentials, so code running as that user can read them (Chrome's newer App-Bound Encryption, starting with cookies, raises that bar). LSASS and SAM need admin or SYSTEM, and other users' home directories are normally not readable.

blocks.question: CISA found NotPetya also infected fully patched Windows machines. What made that possible?
options: Credentials stolen from memory were reused with built-in admin tools (WMIC, PsExec)
EternalBlue worked on patched systems too
It exploited a zero-day in Windows Update
blocks.explain: EternalBlue only worked against unpatched SMBv1. The modified Mimikatz plus WMIC or PsExec route needed no vulnerability, just valid credentials, so patching did nothing to stop it.

lessons.title: Pass-the-hash and pass-the-ticket: why a hash works like a password

blocks.md:
windows-for-security stated that an NTLM hash "works like the password". Here is the reason, straight from Microsoft's protocol specification, so you can see why no amount of password complexity helps once the hash is stolen.

**NTLM** (NT LAN Manager) authenticates with a **challenge-response** mechanism that, in Microsoft's words, "proves to a server or domain controller that a user knows the password associated with an account". Three messages: the client sends NEGOTIATE, the server replies with a CHALLENGE containing a random server challenge, and the client sends AUTHENTICATE with a response computed from a key and that challenge.

blocks.caption: From MS-NLMP (NTLM v2). The response key is derived from the NT hash plus the user and domain names. The proof sent to the server is HMAC_MD5(ResponseKeyNT, ServerChallenge || ...).

blocks.md:
Read the formula slowly. **MD4** (Message Digest 4) is an old hash function; **HMAC** (hash-based message authentication code) combines a key with data. The password appears in exactly one place: inside `MD4(UNICODE(Passwd))`, which is the **NT hash** stored in the SAM and cached in LSASS. Everything else is the user name, the domain name and the server's challenge, which travel over the network or are public.

So whoever holds the NT hash can compute every valid response for that account, for any challenge, forever, without knowing the password. That is **pass-the-hash** (PtH), ATT&CK [T1550.002](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/002/): "authenticating as a user without having access to the user's cleartext password". The hash stays valid until the password changes.

scenes.caption: The intruder holds an admin's NT hash, taken from LSASS on another machine. No password is known.
NTLM starts normally: NEGOTIATE, then the server sends a fresh random challenge.
The response is computed from the NT hash and the challenge, exactly as the real client would. The password itself is never needed.
For a domain account the server asks the domain controller to verify. The DC recomputes from its stored hash and says yes.
Pass-the-ticket: with a stolen Kerberos TGT the intruder asks the DC for service tickets as that user, then presents one to the server.
Either way the server logs a successful network logon by a real account. The evidence is context: which account, from which machine, using which protocol.

blocks.md: **Pass-the-ticket** (PtT, [T1550.003](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/003/)) is the Kerberos version (Kerberos was introduced in windows-for-security). Tickets live in LSASS too. ATT&CK distinguishes two prizes: "A service ticket allows for access to a particular resource, whereas a TGT can be used to request service tickets" for anything the user may access. A **TGT** is the ticket-granting ticket, the first ticket a user receives at logon. A stolen ticket works until it expires. ATT&CK also describes **overpass-the-hash**: using a stolen hash to obtain Kerberos tickets, so turning off NTLM alone does not end hash theft. Forged tickets (golden and silver tickets) and Zerologon belong to active-directory-attacks.

**Microsoft's guard rail for local accounts.** By default, when a member of the local Administrators group connects over the network with a *local* account, "they won't connect as a full administrator" (UAC remote restrictions). Setting the registry value `LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy` to 1 "builds an elevated token" and removes that protection, so audit for it. Domain accounts that are local admins get a full token remotely.

blocks.code:
<!-- Security log on FS01: one network logon (Microsoft field names; values illustrative) -->
<EventID>4624</EventID>
<Data Name="TargetUserName">adm-jlee</Data>
<Data Name="TargetDomainName">CORP</Data>
<Data Name="LogonType">3</Data>
<Data Name="AuthenticationPackageName">NTLM</Data>
<Data Name="LmPackageName">NTLM V2</Data>
<Data Name="WorkstationName">LAPTOP-07</Data>
<Data Name="IpAddress">10.0.4.27</Data>
<Data Name="ElevatedToken">%%1842</Data>   <!-- Yes: administrator session -->
blocks.caption: Defender questions: should adm-jlee ever log on from LAPTOP-07, a user's laptop? Why NTLM, when domain machines normally use Kerberos? Network fields depend on the protocol (Microsoft notes Kerberos network logons may lack a workstation name), so correlate name and address.

blocks.code:
title: Privileged account network logon over NTLM from a non-admin host
id: be017d5e-bcc7-4892-9cb1-a20ef9eac2a4
status: experimental
description: Admin accounts should authenticate with Kerberos from admin workstations.
    An NTLM network logon by one, from anywhere else, deserves a look.
logsource:
    product: windows
    service: security
detection:
    selection:
        EventID: 4624
        LogonType: 3
        AuthenticationPackageName: 'NTLM'
        TargetUserName|startswith: 'adm-'
    filter_admin_workstations:
        WorkstationName|startswith: 'PAW-'
    condition: selection and not filter_admin_workstations
falsepositives:
    - Legacy applications that only speak NTLM
level: medium
tags:
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.t1550.002
blocks.caption: A Sigma rule. Sigma is an open, vendor-neutral format for detection rules (logsource says which logs, detection says what to match, condition combines selections), converted into each SIEM's query language. The adm- and PAW- naming is an example convention; use your own.

blocks.prompt: A company disables NTLM across the domain. Is pass-the-hash now impossible?
blocks.reveal: **No.** ATT&CK's overpass-the-hash uses the same stolen hash "to create a valid Kerberos ticket", which then works for pass-the-ticket. Disabling NTLM removes one channel and is worth doing, but the real fix is to stop the hash being stolen or reusable: Credential Guard, the Protected Users group (which stops RC4 and DES Kerberos keys), unique local passwords and keeping admin credentials off ordinary machines. Lesson 10 covers each.

blocks.md: A hash or ticket is a password-equivalent. Protect where it is cached, make each one valid in as few places as possible, and watch for valid logons in the wrong context: right account, wrong machine, wrong protocol, wrong time.

blocks.question: To pass the hash for a domain account, what does the attacker need?
options: The NT hash, the user name and the domain name
A valid TGT and the password
blocks.explain: The NTLMv2 key is HMAC_MD5 of the NT hash with the upper-cased user name and the domain. The challenge comes from the server. Nothing else is secret.

lessons.title: Credential hygiene: LAPS, Credential Guard, tiers and JIT admin

blocks.md:
You cannot stop every credential from being stolen. The achievable goal is that each stolen credential is **worth little**: unique to one machine, short-lived, and never present on a machine an attacker is likely to control.

Tiny example. Five hundred laptops share one local Administrator password. Steal its hash from one laptop and you hold admin on all five hundred. Give each laptop its own random password and the same theft yields one laptop. The theft did not get harder; it got worthless.

**1. Unique local admin passwords: LAPS.** Microsoft's Windows LAPS (Local Administrator Password Solution) documentation names the problem: "Local administrator accounts often share the same password across many devices, which bad actors can exploit to move laterally". Windows LAPS automatically manages, rotates and backs up each device's local admin password, readable only by authorised administrators. It also manages the DSRM (Directory Services Restore Mode) password on domain controllers.

**2. Keep local accounts off the network.** Microsoft's local accounts guidance: denying local accounts network sign-in "helps to prevent lateral movement" by making sure stolen local credentials cannot be used on other computers. Two well-known SIDs make this name-independent: **S-1-5-113** (Local account) and **S-1-5-114** (Local account and member of Administrators group).

blocks.code:
; Security template excerpt (secedit .inf) for workstations and member servers
[Privilege Rights]
; "Deny access to this computer from the network"
SeDenyNetworkLogonRight = *S-1-5-114
; "Deny log on through Remote Desktop Services"
SeDenyRemoteInteractiveLogonRight = *S-1-5-114

; Credential Guard check (PowerShell, elevated): 1 in the output = running
; (Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_DeviceGuard -Namespace root\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceGuard).SecurityServicesRunning
blocks.caption: The two user-right constants are from Microsoft's policy reference pages. Most organisations set these through Group Policy rather than a raw template; the template shows exactly what the policy stores.

blocks.md: **3. Credential Guard.** It "uses Virtualization-based security (VBS) to isolate secrets", protecting "NTLM password hashes, Kerberos Ticket Granting Tickets (TGTs), and credentials stored by applications as domain credentials". With it on, LSASS talks to an isolated process, `LSAIso.exe`, whose memory the rest of the OS cannot read. It is on by default from Windows 11 22H2 and Windows Server 2025 on domain-joined machines that are not domain controllers and meet the hardware requirements. Limits from the same documentation: it does not protect the Active Directory database on domain controllers, and when enabled, NTLMv1, MS-CHAPv2, Digest and CredSSP cannot use the signed-in credentials. Windows logs System event 13 from WinInit when LsaIso.exe starts.

**4. Protected Users group.** For members, NTLM stops caching the NT hash, Kerberos stops creating DES or RC4 keys and does not cache long-term keys after the first TGT, delegation is refused, and TGTs cannot be renewed beyond their initial four-hour lifetime. Put admin accounts in it; test first, because NTLM-only applications will break for them.

**5. Tiers and admin workstations.** If a domain admin signs in to an ordinary laptop, that laptop now holds a domain admin credential, and every laptop is a path to the domain. Microsoft's **AD tier model** "focused on containing unauthorized escalation of privilege" by splitting administration into tiers; in practice, credentials from a more valuable tier are never used on a less trusted machine. Its successor, the **enterprise access model**, keeps the idea: the old Tier 0 becomes the **control plane** (identity systems such as domain controllers), and the rest splits into a management plane, a data or workload plane, and user and app access.

Admins of the control plane work from a **privileged access workstation** (PAW): Microsoft's highest-security configuration, which blocks email and web browsing, "the most common vector for phishing attacks". For remote desktop to servers, **Remote Credential Guard** redirects Kerberos requests back to the connecting device so credentials "are never passed over the network to the target device".

blocks.title: Why admin credentials must not touch lower tiers

scenes.caption: Three planes of decreasing value. User laptops face phishing every day, so assume some of them are compromised at any time.
The broken habit: a domain admin signs in to a laptop to help a user. Their credential is now cached in that laptop's LSASS.
An intruder on that laptop who reaches SYSTEM takes the credential and goes straight to the control plane. One phish, whole domain.
The tiered habit: control-plane admins use a PAW and never sign in to lower tiers, so no laptop or server ever caches a control-plane credential.

blocks.md: **6. Just-in-time and just-enough admin.** A standing admin account is a credential that is always worth stealing. **Just-in-time** (JIT) access makes privilege temporary: Microsoft Entra (Microsoft's cloud identity service, formerly Azure Active Directory) **Privileged Identity Management** (PIM) offers "just-in-time privileged access", "time-bound access" with start and end dates, approval to activate a role and MFA at activation. **Just Enough Administration** (JEA) narrows what an admin session can do in PowerShell and lets you "reduce the number of administrators on your machines using virtual accounts". Fewer, shorter, narrower privileges mean fewer valuable credentials sitting in memory.

blocks.title: Which control blunts which credential-theft path (simplified)

scenes.caption: Rows are controls from this lesson, columns are theft paths from lesson 8. 1 means the control is designed to stop that path, 0.5 that it limits it, 0 that it does not address it.
Reused local admin hashes are stopped by unique passwords (LAPS) and by refusing local accounts on the network. Credential Guard does not help: the SAM is not what it protects.
Domain credentials in LSASS: Credential Guard isolates them, Protected Users stops NTLM hash caching, tiering keeps them off risky machines. JIT shortens how long they are worth stealing.
Nothing on this list fixes a password left in a script or GPP file. That needs secret scanning and a vault, and changing every password that was exposed.

blocks.question: Which control directly stops a local Administrator hash stolen from one laptop being reused on the other 499?
blocks.explain: LAPS gives every device its own rotating local admin password, so the stolen hash is valid on one machine only. Credential Guard protects domain credentials in LSASS, not local SAM hashes; Protected Users is for domain accounts; Remote Credential Guard protects RDP sessions.

blocks.question: A team enables Credential Guard on its domain controllers and concludes the domain's password hashes are now protected. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: Credential Guard protects all hashes on the machine
Credential Guard does not protect the Active Directory database on domain controllers
Credential Guard only works on Linux
Credential Guard needs Protected Users to be empty
blocks.explain: Microsoft's documentation states Credential Guard does not protect the AD database running on domain controllers, and default enablement covers machines that are not DCs. Domain controllers are protected by tiering: only control-plane admins from PAWs ever touch them.

lessons.title: Discovery: how intruders map a network, and why it is noisy

blocks.md:
An intruder who lands on LAPTOP-07 has no map. Before moving, they need answers: which accounts are admins, which servers exist, which shares are open, which hosts answer on admin ports. **Discovery** (ATT&CK [TA0007](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0007/)) is that information gathering, and ATT&CK notes that "native operating system tools are often used" for it.

Tiny example. Ana opens the finance share every morning: one connection to one file server. Malware on Ana's laptop that wants to find every share in the building tries hundreds of machines in minutes. Same protocol, same port, completely different shape.

**Why it is noisy.** Ordinary users and services have narrow, repetitive habits: the same few servers, the same few ports. Discovery is broad by definition. Two shapes stand out:

1. **Fan-out**: one source contacting many distinct hosts on administrative ports (RPC 135, SMB 445, RDP 3389, WinRM 5985 and 5986) in a short window.
2. **Bursts of built-in commands** from an unusual parent: account, group, domain-trust and share listings run one after another by a process that is not an admin's shell.

The code below measures fan-out from connection records, such as firewall logs, NetFlow (network flow summaries exported by routers) or Sysmon event 3.

blocks.caption: Runnable as shown; the last comment is its actual output. Timestamps are seconds, and window 0 covers the first 10 minutes.

blocks.title: Distinct admin-port peers per source in one 10-minute window

scenes.caption: Normal users: one to two peers each (a file server and a domain controller).
laptop7 touches 40 different hosts on SMB in 40 seconds. No user does that; share enumeration or a worm does.
backup01 also crosses the threshold with 25 servers. It is the backup server doing its job: a known high-fan-out role, to allowlist by name and role.

blocks.md:
**Tuning without going blind.** Backup servers, vulnerability scanners, management and monitoring servers legitimately talk to everything. Allowlist them by *role* (and watch those systems closely, because a compromised management server is an excellent pivot). Do not raise the threshold until the alerts stop: that also hides laptop7.

**Slow discovery** defeats short windows. Add a second view: distinct peers per host per day, compared with that host's own history. A laptop that has never touched more than three servers and today touched thirty is worth a question even if no 10-minute window was busy.

**Prevent:** host firewalls that stop workstations accepting SMB, RPC and WinRM from other workstations (lesson 14) turn discovery into failed connections, which are themselves a loud signal.

blocks.prompt: An intruder spreads the same 40 SMB probes evenly over four hours, one every six minutes. Does the 10-minute, threshold-10 rule above fire?
blocks.reveal: **No.** One probe every 360 seconds puts at most two in any 600-second window, far below 10. That is why the slow, per-day view against the host's own baseline matters: over the day, laptop7 still reaches 40 distinct hosts, against a history of two or three.

blocks.question: backup01 triggers the fan-out alert every night. What is the best response?
options: Delete the rule; it is too noisy
Allowlist backup01 for its known role and destinations, keep the rule for everything else, and monitor backup01 itself closely
blocks.explain: The alert is correct but expected for that role. A targeted exception keeps the signal for every other host. Raising the threshold would also have hidden laptop7, and blocking the backup server breaks backups.

lessons.title: Lateral movement channels and the logs each one leaves

blocks.md:
**Lateral movement** is signing in to another machine with credentials you hold, and running something there. Almost every channel is a normal administration tool, which is the point: ATT&CK's tactic page notes that using legitimate credentials "with native network and operating system tools" may be stealthier than installing new tools.

Tiny example. An IT admin uses remote PowerShell to restart a service on FS01. An intruder holding that admin's hash does exactly the same thing. The target sees a valid network logon and a process start in both cases. The difference is in context: source machine, time, account habits and what ran.

The channels, what happens on the target, and what it writes there:

- **SMB admin shares plus a service** (PsExec-style). Over TCP 445 the tool copies a program to a hidden admin share such as `ADMIN$` ([T1021.002](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/)) and starts it through "a temporary Windows service created through the service control manager API" ([T1569.002](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/)). Target logs: **4624** type 3; **5140** share accessed (if *Audit File Share* is on); **7045** / **4697** service installed; a process whose parent is `services.exe`. PsExec is a Sysinternals tool for running processes on other machines.

- **WMI** (Windows Management Instrumentation, Windows' management interface): remote WMI travels over DCOM (Distributed Component Object Model) on port 135, or over WinRM ([T1047](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1047/)). Target: 4624 type 3; new processes whose parent is the WMI Provider Host, `wmiprvse.exe`.
- **WinRM / PowerShell remoting** (Windows Remote Management, ports 5985 HTTP and 5986 HTTPS, [T1021.006](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/006/)): 4624 type 3; with script block logging on, PowerShell **4104** records the script.

- **RDP** ([T1021.001](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/001/)): an interactive desktop over TCP 3389; 4624 **type 10** (RemoteInteractive), plus the *Restricted Admin Mode* field (Yes when the client connected in Restricted Admin mode, which does not hand reusable credentials to the server).
- **SSH** ([T1021.004](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/004/)): Linux auth logs record `Accepted publickey` or `Accepted password` with the source address (linux-for-security). Modern Windows also ships an SSH server.
- **Cloud consoles and APIs** ([T1021.007](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/007/)): many enterprises federate on-premises identities to the cloud, so a stolen domain credential may log in to the cloud control plane. The trail is in the cloud's audit log; AWS CloudTrail, for example, records actions "taken in the AWS Management Console, AWS Command Line Interface, and AWS SDKs and APIs".

Every channel needs an account the target accepts. That is why lessons 8 to 10 come before this one: credential hygiene shrinks the number of channels that work at all.

blocks.title: Which log signal each movement channel produces on the target

scenes.caption: Simplified map of the main signals on the target host. Dark cells mean the channel normally produces that event, given the audit settings from windows-for-security.
SMB plus service creation is the loudest: a network logon, a new service and a process started by services.exe, within seconds.
Network logons (type 3) are shared by SMB, WMI and WinRM. On their own they are everyday noise; the process that follows tells them apart.
RDP is the one Windows channel with its own logon type (10). SSH lives in a different log entirely, so collect Linux auth logs too.

blocks.title: One PsExec-style hop as an event stream on the target (illustrative)

scenes.caption: t = 0 s: a network logon by an admin account from LAPTOP-07 (4624, type 3), with 4672 listing its special privileges.
t = 1 s: the hidden ADMIN$ share is accessed (5140) and a new executable appears in the Windows folder (Sysmon 11).
t = 3 s: the service control manager installs a new service pointing at that file (System 7045; Security 4697 if auditing is on).
t = 4 s: the service starts: its binary runs as a child of services.exe and starts the requested command (4688, Sysmon 1).
Read as a sequence, eight events in about five seconds tell one story. Any one alone is ordinary; the chain from one source account is not.

blocks.code:
title: Service installed from outside the usual program folders
id: dd773c1e-aac1-4311-a964-6f92e7a678da
status: experimental
description: Remote execution tools often install a short-lived service whose binary
    sits in the Windows folder or a temp path rather than Program Files or System32.
logsource:
    product: windows
    service: system
detection:
    selection:
        Provider_Name: 'Service Control Manager'
        EventID: 7045
    usual_locations:
        ImagePath|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
            - '\Windows\System32\'
    condition: selection and not usual_locations
falsepositives:
    - Agents and installers that place service binaries elsewhere (allowlist them)
level: medium
tags:
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.t1569.002
blocks.caption: Field names follow the SigmaHQ repository's System-log rules. SigmaHQ also maintains a narrower rule that matches the PsExec service by its name, PSEXESVC; layered rules catch both the known tool and its look-alikes.

blocks.md: **SSH has its own credential trap: agent forwarding.** An SSH agent holds your unlocked private keys. With agent forwarding on, a server you connect to can ask your agent to sign logins onward. The `ssh_config(5)` manual warns that users who can bypass file permissions on that server "can access the local agent through the forwarded connection": they cannot copy the key, but "they can perform operations on the keys that enable them to authenticate using the identities loaded into the agent". A root intruder on a jump host can therefore ride every admin who forwards an agent through it. Prefer `ProxyJump`, which connects to the jump host and then opens a TCP forward to the destination, so authentication to the final server happens from your own machine.

blocks.question: On a file server you see 4624 type 3 from an admin account, then 7045 for a service called `XYZSVC` with an image path in `C:\Windows\`, then a process started by services.exe. What happened most likely?
options: Someone logged in at the console
A remote execution tool used SMB and a temporary service to run a command
blocks.explain: A network logon followed by a freshly installed service and a child of services.exe is the SMB-plus-service pattern (T1021.002 with T1569.002). Console logons are type 2, RDP is type 10, and scheduled tasks write their own events.

blocks.question: Which logon type separates an RDP session from SMB, WMI or WinRM access in 4624?
blocks.explain: RDP produces type 10 (RemoteInteractive). SMB, WMI and WinRM all produce type 3 (Network), so for those you need the events that follow to tell them apart.

lessons.title: Pivoting and tunnelling: reaching networks you cannot reach

blocks.md:
Firewalls divide networks into zones. An intruder's own computer on the internet usually cannot reach the internal database or the domain controllers at all. **Pivoting** means using a compromised machine as a stepping stone: it can reach places the attacker cannot, so the attacker sends traffic *through* it.

Tiny example. A company's web server sits in a DMZ (demilitarised zone: a network segment between the internet and the internal network). The internet can reach the web server on port 443. The web server can reach the database on port 5432 because the application needs it. Nothing on the internet can reach port 5432. Once the web server is compromised, it becomes the attacker's relay to everything the web server is allowed to talk to.

ATT&CK describes two related techniques:

- **Internal proxy** ([T1090.001](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1090/001/)): a compromised system relays command-and-control traffic for others, to "reduce the number of simultaneous outbound network connections", survive connection loss, or "ride over existing trusted communications paths". Peer-to-peer relays over SMB blend into normal Windows traffic.
- **Protocol tunnelling** ([T1572](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1572/)): "explicitly encapsulating a protocol within another", for example SSH tunnelling (SSH port forwarding).
