It can hide traffic inside an allowed protocol and reach "otherwise unreachable systems", such as SMB or RDP that firewalls would filter.

A **tunnel** hides what is inside it, not that it exists. Its outer connection still has a source, a destination, a duration and a byte count.

blocks.title: A pivot through the DMZ, and where defenders see it

scenes.caption: Direct connections from the internet to internal admin ports are dropped at the perimeter. This is what segmentation is for.
The web server is reachable on 443 and is allowed to reach the database. After compromise, the attacker carries their traffic inside a tunnel to it.
If the DMZ firewall also lets the web server reach the domain controller, the relay extends there: RDP and SMB from a web server.
Defender view: a web server opening RDP or SMB to a DC is a source and destination pair it never had. Egress rules should refuse it and flow logs should flag it.

blocks.md:
**What pivoting leaves behind:**
- **New connection pairs.** A server that suddenly talks to hosts or ports it never used. Flow logs and firewall logs show this without decrypting anything.
- **Long-lived connections with steady, small traffic**, typical of interactive sessions or relays rather than web requests.
- **New listening ports or relay processes** on the compromised host (Sysmon event 3 for connections, and a comparison with the host's normal listeners).
- **SSH sessions carrying forwards** on Linux jump hosts.

**Prevent:** give every server an **egress** (outbound) policy that allows only what its job needs, so a compromised web server can reach its database and nothing else. On SSH servers that are not meant to be jump hosts, disable forwarding.

blocks.caption: nftables is the Linux kernel's packet filter. DisableForwarding turns off TCP, agent, X11 and socket forwarding in sshd. sshd_config(5) adds a caveat: disabling forwarding does not help much if users still have a shell and can run their own forwarders, so the egress policy does the real work.

blocks.prompt: The egress policy above is in place and the web server is compromised. The attacker tries to reach the domain controller's SMB port through it. What do defenders get?
blocks.reveal: The connection is **refused**, and the `egress-drop` log line records a source (the web server), a destination (the DC) and port 445 that this server has no reason to use. A blocked attempt like that is a high-quality alert: almost no false positives, and it arrives at the moment the intruder starts pivoting, before anything internal is touched.

blocks.question: Why does protocol tunnelling not make the activity invisible to network defenders?
options: The outer connection still shows its endpoints, timing, duration and volume
Firewalls decrypt all SSH traffic by default
blocks.explain: Encapsulation hides the inner protocol, not the outer flow. A web server holding a long SSH session to an unusual host, or moving steady traffic for hours, stands out in flow and firewall logs without any decryption.

lessons.title: Defending the path: segmentation, admin hygiene, EDR, HSE timeline

blocks.md:
No single control stops a post-foothold intrusion. The working approach is to put an obstacle and a sensor at **every** link of the chain from lesson 1, so the intruder has to win many times in a row while you only have to notice once and act.

The US advisories in this course converge on the same short list. For Conti, CISA, the FBI and the NSA recommended multifactor authentication, "robust network segmentation", timely patching, removing unneeded remote-access tools, endpoint detection and response tools, restricting RDP, and auditing admin accounts under "least privilege and separation of duties". For NotPetya, CISA advised host-based firewalls that "block workstation-to-workstation communications", disabling or limiting remote WMI and file sharing, and limiting who holds admin rights.

Mapped to the chain:

- **Escalation:** the Linux and Windows audits from lessons 2 to 7 on a schedule; patch known-exploited bugs first. CISA tracks them in its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue; CISA closed PrintNightmare's emergency directive and moved its required actions to BOD 22-01, the directive behind that catalogue.
- **Credential access:** Credential Guard, LSA protection, Protected Users, LAPS, no secrets in files (lessons 8 to 10).
- **Discovery:** fan-out and command-burst detection (lesson 11).
- **Lateral movement:** workstations do not accept admin protocols from other workstations; admins work from PAWs with just-in-time rights; the event chains from lesson 12 are alerts.
- **Everywhere:** **EDR** (endpoint detection and response: security software on each host that records what runs there and can alert and respond; CISA says such tools "allow a high degree of visibility into the security status of endpoints") and central log collection that the intruder cannot erase from the host.

blocks.code:
# Workstations: refuse SMB, RPC, WinRM and RDP from the workstation subnet (PowerShell, admin)
# Deploy through Group Policy in practice; servers and admin PAWs keep their own rules.
New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'Block admin protocols from workstations' `
  -Direction Inbound -Action Block -Protocol TCP `
  -LocalPort 135, 445, 3389, 5985, 5986 `
  -RemoteAddress 10.0.4.0/22

# Check what is now enforced
Get-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'Block admin protocols from workstations' |
  Get-NetFirewallPortFilter
blocks.caption: One rule implements CISA's NotPetya advice to block workstation-to-workstation traffic for the ports in this course. Test it first: some helpdesk tools rely on these ports and need an exception from their own management hosts only.

blocks.md: **Case: Colonial Pipeline and DarkSide (May 2021).** Joseph Blount, Colonial's CEO, told the US Senate that the company found a ransom note on 7 May 2021 and halted the pipeline to keep the malware away from the operational technology (OT: the systems that control physical equipment). Blount's testimony says the attacker "exploited a legacy virtual private network (VPN) profile that was not intended to be in use". CISA's advisory on the incident stressed "robust network segmentation between IT and OT networks" and reported "no indications that the threat actor moved laterally to OT systems". Two lessons: forgotten remote access is a foothold, and segmentation is what kept the intrusion in IT.

**Case: the Conti playbook.** CISA reports that a leaked Conti playbook told affiliates to escalate and move laterally with three known bugs: the 2017 SMBv1 vulnerabilities, PrintNightmare (lesson 7) and **Zerologon** (CVE-2020-1472), a flaw in the Netlogon protocol of domain controllers that is covered in active-directory-attacks (found by Tom Tervoort of the security firm Secura, now part of Bureau Veritas; [their write-up](https://www.secura.com/blog/zero-logon)). Every one had a patch. Criminal playbooks favour old, patched bugs because many networks have not applied the fix.

blocks.title: The HSE intrusion, day by day from the phishing email (16 March 2021)

scenes.caption: Day 0: phishing email with a malicious Excel file. Day 2 (18 March): it is opened and patient zero is infected. Day 7: persistence is added.
Day 15 (31 March): antivirus detects Cobalt Strike and Mimikatz on patient zero. It is in monitor mode, so nothing is blocked, and no investigation starts.
Days 16 to 51: the response provider found no significant attacker activity. Day 52 (7 May): AD reconnaissance, privileged accounts used, first servers compromised.
Days 53 to 57: hospitals are compromised. Hospital C asks about Cobalt Strike alerts (day 55) and is told the risk is low. Hospital A's responders reset 4,500 passwords (day 57).
Day 58: a provider emails that threats went unhandled on at least 16 systems since 7 May. Day 59 (14 May, 01:00): Conti runs. Several sensors fired; the response never caught up.

blocks.md: Read the HSE timeline as a defender. There was an eight-week window and at least three detections. PwC also records that the Department of Health, "a third party to the HSE's environment", "successfully acted on a detection" and prevented the ransomware across the vast majority of its systems. The difference was not the sensor; it was whether a detection became an investigation. That is why this course pairs every technique with what it leaves behind: evidence only matters if someone is expected to act on it.

Escalation and lateral movement are a chain of small, valid-looking steps. Make each step harder (least privilege, unique and protected credentials, segmentation, patching known-exploited bugs) and make each step visible (forwarded logs, EDR, the event chains in this course), then make sure every alert has an owner.

**Practise legally.** Only test systems you own or have written permission to test.

- [EVTX-ATTACK-SAMPLES](https://github.com/sbousseaden/EVTX-ATTACK-SAMPLES): Windows event logs recorded during attack techniques, in folders by ATT&CK tactic, including Privilege Escalation, Credential Access and Lateral Movement. Practise reading 4624, 7045 and Sysmon chains.
- [OTRF Security-Datasets](https://github.com/OTRF/Security-Datasets): recorded security events from simulated attacks, to replay and hunt through.
- [SigmaHQ rules](https://github.com/SigmaHQ/sigma): the public Sigma rule repository; read the rules for the techniques in this course and test them on the datasets above.
- [Blue Team Labs Online](https://blueteamlabs.online/): investigation challenges for defenders.
- [Hack The Box](https://www.hackthebox.com/): legal practice machines where Linux and Windows privilege escalation can be tried hands-on, then compared with the logs they leave.

blocks.question: PwC found several detections in the HSE network weeks before the ransomware ran. What was the main failure?
options: There were no security tools at all
The attacker used an unknown zero-day exploit
Logs were encrypted by the ransomware before anyone could see them
Detections did not lead to an investigation and response in time
blocks.explain: Antivirus saw Cobalt Strike and Mimikatz on 31 March, hospitals saw alerts in May, and a provider flagged unhandled threats the day before. None became an incident investigation in time. Where the Department of Health did act, the ransomware was largely prevented.

blocks.question: CISA reported no indication that the DarkSide actors moved laterally from Colonial's IT network to OT. Which control does that point to?
options: Segmentation between IT and OT networks
blocks.explain: CISA's advisory stressed robust IT/OT segmentation so attackers cannot pivot to OT even if IT is compromised. Colonial still shut the pipeline as a precaution, which shows how much the IT side mattered operationally.
